questions.subject: Reading
questions.learningObjective: Interpret details, vocabulary and relationships in a short expository passage.
questions.passageTitle: Reading the age of a pottery deposit
questions.passage:
Archaeologists sometimes find several styles of pottery in the same deposit. A decorated bowl associated with an early period and a plainer cup associated with a later one may lie side by side. Dating the deposit from the bowl alone would assume that the inhabitants discarded it soon after it was made. Yet a well-made bowl can remain in use for years, and even broken pieces can be moved when soil from an earlier settlement is used to level a later building site.

In an undisturbed deposit, the youngest securely identified object places a lower limit on the date of deposition. For example, if the cup style first appeared around 1450, the deposit containing the cup could have formed around 1450 or later. The cup alone cannot set an upper limit, since people could have kept making or using cups of that style long after its introduction.

The word “securely” matters. A burrowing animal or a later posthole can introduce a young fragment into an old layer. Before relying on the fragment, archaeologists examine the surrounding soil, look for boundaries that cut through the layer, and compare it with finds from nearby undisturbed deposits. Dates become more persuasive when the objects and the physical evidence from the site support the same interpretation.
questions.prompt: What assumption would an archaeologist make by dating the deposit from the decorated bowl alone?
questions.answer: The bowl was discarded relatively soon after it was made.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph identifies the assumption and explains how continued use or moving older soil can break it.
options: The cup had been brought from a distant settlement.
The bowl and cup had been made from the same clay.
The bowl was discarded relatively soon after it was made.
The cup style was more durable than the bowl style.

questions.passageTitle: Why a courtyard can cool after sunset
questions.passage:
Two paved courtyards can register similar air temperatures in mid-afternoon yet feel quite different after sunset. A thick masonry surface absorbs energy during the day and may release some of it into the evening. A thinner surface can heat rapidly in sunlight but has less material in which to store energy. Its daytime surface temperature alone therefore provides an incomplete guide to how much warmth it will give back later.

The shape of the courtyard also matters. An open courtyard has a broad view of the sky, which allows its surfaces to lose energy through infrared radiation on a clear night. In a narrow courtyard, tall walls interrupt much of that view. The paving still radiates energy, but it also receives infrared radiation from the surrounding walls. If the walls remain warm, this exchange reduces the paving’s net heat loss compared with a similar surface facing a clear sky.

An investigator interested in why one courtyard cools more slowly could record paving temperatures at intervals after sunset. Comparing only courtyards with different paving and different wall heights would make it difficult to attribute the difference to either factor. Comparing two courtyards with the same paving but different degrees of enclosure would give clearer evidence about the role of the walls.
questions.prompt: What distinction does the first paragraph draw between the two types of paving?
questions.answer: A surface can get hot quickly while storing relatively little energy.
questions.explanation: The thinner surface may become hot quickly even though its smaller mass limits stored energy.
options: Both pavements necessarily retain equal energy when the air temperature matches.
A surface can get hot quickly while storing relatively little energy.
Thicker paving can release energy only while it receives sunlight.
A thinner layer must remain cooler than a thicker layer all afternoon.

questions.passageTitle: How a museum catalog can bias a search
questions.passage:
A museum catalog provides access to collections by assigning searchable terms to objects. These terms may look like a neutral index, but they often reflect the institution’s earlier collecting priorities. For example, records for handwoven cloth may name the donor and the region of acquisition while omitting the weaving technique. A search by donor then retrieves many records. A search by technique retrieves far fewer, even if the museum holds many relevant pieces.

Adding richer terminology can improve access, but the task involves more than attaching new words. Different communities may use the same term for different weaving methods. Historical records may use several spellings for one name, while a preferred term in a modern catalog may have been absent from the original paperwork. A catalog can preserve the historical wording and link it to an additional searchable term, so that users can find the record from either starting point.

Blank fields require particular care. When an item has no technique recorded, the blank may mean that the technique has not yet been identified. It could also mean that the technique has been identified but not entered in the catalog. A researcher comparing search results should therefore check how records were made and updated before treating the number of matches as a count of the museum’s holdings.
questions.prompt: Why might a search by donor return more records than a search by weaving technique?
questions.answer: Donor names may have been recorded more consistently than techniques.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph describes how cataloging priorities can make one field more complete than another.
options: Donated cloth is usually made using a wider range of techniques.
The catalog automatically combines technique results under donor names.
Cloth without recorded techniques is kept in a different institution.
Donor names may have been recorded more consistently than techniques.
